NTSB:20200616X02410.s: The pilot of an aerial application aircraft likely exceeded the critical angle of attack while maneuvering at low altitude. This caused an aerodynamic stall, spin, and loss of control, resulting in a nose-first descent and crash.

NTSB:20200616X52914.n: During landing, while at about 1,200 ft above ground level, the airplane's engine lost all power. Subsequently, the airplane landed short of the lake on the land and came to rest nosed down. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage. An FAA postaccident examination revealed that about 15.5 gallons of clean blue fuel was drained from the airplane, and that there was fuel in the firewall drain sump. It was noted that two small "pearls" of water were observed in the fuel collection cup. A picture supplied of the airplane after the accident showed that the carburetor heat was found not applied. The engine was test run and revealed no mechanical failure or malfunctions. The pilot reported that he did not recall if he had applied carburetor heat during the approach to land prior to the loss of engine power. The temperature and dew point were entered into a carburetor icing probability chart, which coincided with the "serious icing-glide power" category.
NTSB:20200616X52914.s: During landing at 1,200 feet, the pilot experienced total engine power loss, resulting in a short landing with substantial fuselage damage. The investigation attributed the failure to probable carburetor icing, as carburetor heat was not applied despite conditions indicating a serious icing risk.

NTSB:20200616X82840.n: The pilot was conducting a straight in approach to the runway in turbulent, gusty wind conditions. During the approach, he did not verify that he had extended the airplane's retractable landing gear. As the flared the airplane during the landing, he heard the landing gear warning horn, but it was too late to go-around. He subsequently landed the airplane with the landing gear retracted. The airplane's lower fuselage was substantially damaged. The pilot reported that there were no mechanical anomalies with the airframe or engine that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20200616X82840.s: The pilot landed an airplane with the landing gear retracted during a straight-in approach in turbulent winds after failing to verify gear extension. The aircraft sustained substantial lower fuselage damage, though the pilot reported no mechanical anomalies.

NTSB:20200616X82852.n: The pilot of a tailwheel-equipped airplane reported that during the day he practiced several landings with no anomalies. He picked up a passenger and attempted a full stop landing at a nearby airport. Shortly after touchdown, the airplane nose turned slightly to the right. The pilot corrected with rudder input to the left, and the airplane turned sharply to the left. He stated that he could not correct the left turn with the rudder or wheel brakes, and the airplane exited the left side of the runway. The right wing and right horizontal stabilizer contacted terrain, and the airplane came to rest upright. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the right wing and the elevator. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20200616X82852.s: The pilot of a tailwheel-equipped airplane exited the left side of the runway shortly after touchdown during a full stop landing with a passenger. Despite rudder and brake inputs, the aircraft turned sharply left, sustaining substantial damage to the right wing and elevator, with no preaccident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20200616X84617.n: The BEA of France has notified the NTSB of an incident involving a Bombardier CL600-2C10 airplane that occurred on January 23, 2020. The NTSB has appointed a U.S. Accredited Representative to assist the BEA of France's investigation under the provisions of ICAO Annex 13.All investigative information will be released by the BEA of France.
NTSB:20200616X84617.s: The BEA of France notified the NTSB of an incident involving a Bombardier CL600-2C10 on January 23, 2020. The NTSB appointed a U.S. Accredited Representative to assist the investigation, with all information to be released by the BEA.

NTSB:20200617X32049.n: The pilot reported that upon lifting off in the powered parachute, he noticed two riser lines were twisted which impaired his ability to control the aircraft. The aircraft subsequently struck a tree and sustained minor damage while the pilot was attempting to land. The pilot was seriously injured. He noted that completing a better parachute layout during his preflight inspection might have prevented the accident.
NTSB:20200617X32049.s: The pilot of a powered parachute reported that twisted riser lines impaired control after lift-off, causing the aircraft to strike a tree and sustain minor damage during landing. The pilot was seriously injured and attributed the accident to an inadequate preflight parachute layout.

NTSB:20200617X52807.n: The pilot reported that he encountered moderate to severe turbulence below 5,000 ft mean sea level while descending to land on runway 30. During the landing flare the left wing abruptly raised up. The airplane touched down hard and bounced. The airplane settled down, the nose wheel collapsed, and the airplane skidded to a stop. The engine mount sustained substantial damage. The prevailing wind was from 230° at 11 knots gusting to 15 knots.
NTSB:20200617X52807.s: The pilot encountered moderate to severe turbulence below 5,000 ft while descending to land on runway 30. A hard landing and bounce caused the nose wheel to collapse, resulting in substantial engine mount damage.

NTSB:20200617X61443.n: The government of India has notified the NTSB of an accident involving a CESSNA 152 airplane that occurred on June 08, 2020. The NTSB has appointed a U.S. Accredited Representative to assist the government of India's investigation under the provisions of ICAO Annex 13.All investigative information will be released by the government of India.
NTSB:20200617X61443.s: The Government of India notified the NTSB of a Cessna 152 accident on June 08, 2020. The NTSB appointed a U.S. Accredited Representative to assist the investigation, with all information to be released by the Government of India.

NTSB:20200617X61630.n: The pilot stated that he hand-started the engine by turning the propeller from behind. The airplane was not chocked, but the pilot stated he had "moved the tail wheel sideways." The engine started immediately, and the airplane collided with a utility pole, causing leading edge damage to both wings.
NTSB:20200617X61630.s: The pilot hand-started the unchocked engine by turning the propeller from behind, moving the tail wheel sideways. The aircraft immediately collided with a utility pole, causing leading edge damage to both wings.

NTSB:20200617X70035.n: During the landing, the airplane floated down the runway in an unusually nose high attitude. The pilot responded by abruptly lowering the nose of the airplane, and the airplane landed hard and bounced. He then increased and decreased the engine power setting and the airplane touched down hard again. The right main landing gear collapsed, and the airplane exited the runway to the left before it came to rest upright in a grass field. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the engine mounts and truss. The pilot reported that there were no preimpact mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. He also reported that following the accident, he calculated the weight of the baggage and determined that the airplane's center of gravity was at the aft limit.
NTSB:20200617X70035.s: The pilot landed an airplane with an aft-limit center of gravity, causing it to float nose-high and bounce. Subsequent power adjustments led to a hard touchdown, collapsing the right main gear and forcing the aircraft off the runway into a grass field with substantial damage.

NTSB:20200617X85704.n: According to the pilot of the helicopter, he was flying low-level about 20 mph, pollinating a rice field. He reported that he misjudged his operating altitude, and the helicopter contacted the rice vegetation. The helicopter entered an uncontrollable spin and impacted the rice field. The pilot reported that he was unharmed, but the helicopter was "totally destroyed". He added that the helicopter was operating normally, and the accident was due to "pilot error" in misjudging his altitude.
NTSB:20200617X85704.s: The helicopter pilot misjudged operating altitude while pollinating a rice field at low level and 20 mph, causing the aircraft to contact vegetation. This resulted in an uncontrollable spin and total destruction of the helicopter, though the pilot remained unharmed.

NTSB:20200618X02326.n: The pilot reported that, during an aerial application flight, a partial loss of engine power occurred while he was performing the first climbing turn to reverse course. The airplane subsequently descended and impacted terrain in a near-vertical attitude. Postaccident examination of the engine and its components revealed no preimpact anomalies. The reason for the partial loss of engine power could not be determined with the available evidence for this accident investigation. Given the airplane's near-vertical descent, it is likely that the pilot exceeded the airplane's critical angle of attack during the climbing turn, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall and a loss of airplane control from which the pilot was unable to recover.
NTSB:20200618X02326.s: During an aerial application flight, the pilot experienced partial engine power loss while climbing to reverse course, causing the aircraft to impact terrain. Investigators could not determine the power loss cause but concluded the pilot likely stalled due to exceeding the critical angle of attack.

NTSB:20200618X13408.n: After performing an engine runup, the private pilot initiated the takeoff roll within allowable weight limits. When the flight was about midway along the 2,600 ft long grass runway at a lesser than normal indicated airspeed for that point along the runway, he thought about aborting but elected to continue and rotated at 50 knots near the departure end of the runway. The airplane remained in ground effect, and he pushed the yoke to increase airspeed while flying through a gap in trees past the departure end of the runway. The airplane reached an airspeed of 50 to 55 knots and climbed to an altitude of about 35 ft above ground level; however, it subsequently struck trees, stalled, and impacted the ground resulting in a small postcrash fire in the engine compartment area due to a broken carburetor. Postaccident examination of the engine revealed no preimpact anomalies. Although the pilot later attributed the poor performance to his initiating the takeoff with the ignition switch positioned to one magneto rather than both, it was in the off position when first viewed by recovery personnel 2 days later.
NTSB:20200618X13408.s: A private pilot attempted a takeoff on a grass runway at low airspeed, rotated early, and struck trees while climbing. The aircraft stalled and crashed with a post-impact fire caused by a broken carburetor, though the pilot's claim of using only one magneto could not be verified.

NTSB:20200618X83813.n: The pilot was applying insecticide to a farm field and the accident flight was the first time the pilot had sprayed the field. Once he arrived at the site, 3 hours late, the pilot conducted two circular passes to survey the field, then landed, and the ground crew loaded the insecticide into the hopper. The pilot was not briefed of any hazards to operations prior to the flight by the ground crew or farmer. After takeoff, the pilot started applying the chemicals. The helicopter was performing the spraying operation and was flying on a northerly heading when it impacted a non-energized wire. The wire was mounted about 30 feet up a 40 ft pole that also contained a hunting stand and stretched about 250 ft across the field from west to east where it connected to a tree bordering the field. The wire had been installed at least 20 years earlier and was installed high enough that a tractor or combine had clearance to move beneath it during harvest. Clear daylight conditions existed at the time of the accident. The sun was at 39.85° above the horizon at an azimuth of 272.39° and was very close to being directly in line with the wire. It is possible that the sun’s position relative to the wire would have made the 5/16-inch wire more difficult to see as the shadow of the wire and pole would have been nearly directly under the wire rather than offset. The pilot, unfamiliar with the field, running late, and without the benefit of a detailed discussion with the landowner, relied solely on his brief visual surveillance of the field while operating the helicopter. Although the pilot likely observed the pole and hunting stand during his surveillance, it is likely that he did not see the wire due to its small diameter. Therefore, shortly after initiating the application of the insecticide, the pilot’s failure to see and avoid the wire resulted in the helicopter impacting the wire and the pilot’s subsequent loss of control and impact with terrain.
NTSB:20200618X83813.s: A pilot flying a helicopter during an insecticide spraying operation impacted a non-energized wire due to poor visibility caused by sun glare and lack of hazard briefing. The collision resulted in a loss of control and impact with terrain.

NTSB:20200618X91338.n: The airplane was on final approach for landing, with the landing gear extended, when the landing gear indication light in the cockpit started to flicker. After a few seconds, the light became solid. The pilot visually verified that all three landing gear were extended and then proceeded to land. Upon touchdown, the left main landing gear (MLG) collapsed. The airplane slid off the runway and came to rest in the adjacent field, resulting in substantial damage to the wings. A postaccident examination of the landing gear system revealed several discrepancies, including missing cotter pins and other hardware, improper tension on the landing gear downlocks, and mis-rigging of the landing gear actuator. Because the most recent maintenance for the landing gear system was documented 15 days before the accident, it is likely these discrepancies were not addressed during the maintenance (which included a main landing gear wheel, tire, and brake inspection). The most severe discrepancy was likely the mis-rigged condition of the retraction system, which would have allowed the left main landing gear to enter an overcenter position and collapse during landing.
NTSB:20200618X91338.s: The pilot landed an aircraft on final approach after a flickering gear light, but the left main landing gear collapsed on touchdown, causing the airplane to slide off the runway with substantial wing damage. Post-accident examination attributed the collapse to maintenance discrepancies, specifically a mis-rigged retraction system that allowed the gear to enter an overcenter position.

NTSB:20200619X12749.n: The pilot stated that during landing in gusting wind conditions, the tailwheel-equipped airplane lost rudder authority as it slowed down in the landing roll. A strong gust of wind caused the airplane to weather-vane and ground-loop. The right wing hit the ground and the right main landing gear collapsed which resulted in substantial damage to the right aileron. The pilot stated there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20200619X12749.s: The pilot reported that a tailwheel-equipped airplane weather-vaned and ground-looped during the landing roll in gusting winds after losing rudder authority. The right wing struck the ground, collapsing the right main gear and damaging the aileron, with no preimpact mechanical failures.
